parts.problem_md:
How is the relationship between Ed and Judy Boone presented in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time, Simon Stephens presents the relationship between Ed and Judy Boone as tense and emotional, shaped by misunderstanding, guilt, and their shared love for their son, Christopher. Their relationship is damaged but not beyond repair. Through the play, Stephens explores how poor communication, emotional stress, and absence affect their bond, while also showing that they may be able to rebuild some trust through their care for Christopher.

At the start of the play, we learn that Ed and Judy’s marriage has already broken down. Ed has lied to Christopher about Judy, telling him “your mother’s died”. While this seems cruel, it comes from a place of fear and love. Ed wants to protect Christopher from the painful truth of being left. His decision shows how much he struggles with his own feelings and with what’s best for his son.

Judy’s point of view is shown in the letters Christopher finds hidden in Ed’s wardrobe. In these, she admits her mistakes and shows her love for her son. She writes, “I was not a very good mother, Christopher. Maybe if things had been different, maybe if you’d been different, I might have been better at it.” This helps the audience understand that she didn’t stop caring for him — she was just overwhelmed. She also says, “I thought what I was doing was the best for all of us”, showing she still wants to be part of his life.

When Ed and Judy see each other again in London, their emotions run high. Judy is angry that Ed lied to Christopher and says, “What in God’s name did you think you were playing at saying those things to him?” Ed replies by listing all the things he did for Christopher on his own: “I cooked his meals. I cleaned his clothes… And you?” These arguments show how much pain and blame there is between them, but also how much they’ve both struggled.

Even though their relationship is full of tension, we also see moments where they work together for Christopher’s sake. For example, when Christopher refuses to talk to Ed about his Maths A Level, Judy acts as mediator and encourages Christopher to respond to his father. This shows that both parents still care deeply for their son and are starting to cooperate, even if they aren’t close anymore.

Stephens also uses form and structure to explore their relationship. As the play is told through Christopher’s point of view, with help from Siobhan, we see Judy and Ed through his eyes. This makes their actions seem more confusing at times, but also helps us understand how hard it is for Christopher to make sense of adult emotions. Stage directions add more meaning too — for example, when Ed shouts, “I will not have that man’s name mentioned in my house”, it shows how upset he is about Judy’s relationship with Mr Shears. When Christopher starts drumming to block out his parents’ argument, it shows how deeply their conflict affects him.

More broadly, the play shows how hard it can be to raise a neurodivergent child, especially in a world that doesn’t always offer support. Ed and Judy’s relationship breaks down not because they don’t love their son, but because they feel tired, alone, and unsure how to cope. Stephens doesn’t make either parent the villain — instead, he shows them as real people in a difficult situation.

In conclusion, Stephens presents Ed and Judy’s relationship as complicated and emotional. Their past is full of mistakes, but their care for Christopher brings moments of hope. Through language, structure, and stage direction, Stephens shows that while their relationship isn’t perfect, it’s still real and may begin to heal. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. The response maintains a critical and engaged tone throughout, showing empathy and insight into both characters. The candidate draws on a wide range of evidence, including dialogue and stage directions, and integrates this fluently into their argument. There is a clear personal engagement with the emotional complexity of the relationship, supported by thoughtful interpretations. > > The structure is well-balanced, with a sustained and developed argument. parts.problem_md:
‘Christopher, Ed, Judy and Mrs Shears all try to cope with loss in different ways.’

Explore how different types of loss are dealt with in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

Simon Stephens’s adaptation of The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time explores the theme of loss in powerful and contrasting ways. Throughout the play, we see how different characters deal with various kinds of loss: the loss of loved ones, trust, stability, and even pets. Stephens uses dialogue, structure, and staging to help the audience understand how complex and personal the experience of loss can be.

At the start of the play, there is a shocking and sudden loss: Wellington the dog has been killed. This event deeply upsets both Christopher and Mrs Shears, but they react very differently. Mrs Shears is overwhelmed and reacts with “Oh no”, showing how much she relied on the dog for emotional comfort. Wellington was more than just a pet — he filled a gap left by people who had left her life. Later, it is revealed that Ed, Christopher’s father, killed the dog. He did this not out of hatred for the dog, but because he was angry and upset about losing his relationship with Mrs Shears. Ed couldn’t deal with his feelings properly and acted out in a violent way. This shows how grief can lead to destructive behaviour when it is not understood or processed.

Christopher, on the other hand, deals with the loss of Wellington in a completely different way. He doesn’t cry or show much emotion. Instead, he decides to investigate: “I want to find out who killed Wellington”. This makes sense for his character, as he sees the world through facts, logic, and patterns. Solving the mystery helps him make sense of something painful. His reaction is also seen when he is told that his mother has died. Instead of showing sadness, he asks, “What kind of heart attack?” and says, “It was probably an aneurysm”. These responses show that Christopher copes with emotional moments by thinking scientifically. It doesn’t mean he isn’t affected, but that his way of managing grief is different from what many people might expect.

Judy, Christopher’s mother, also suffers from loss in the play. She leaves her family, but it’s clear she didn’t stop loving her son. In one of her letters, she admits, “Maybe if things had been different… I might have been better at it”. This shows she feels guilty and regrets not being there. When Christopher appears at her flat in London, she acts immediately: “Come downstairs. Bring Toby. Get into the car”. Even though she left, she still sees herself as a mother and wants to protect Christopher. When her relationship with Mr Shears breaks down later in the play, Judy doesn’t dwell on it — she takes action by moving out and starting again with her son. This suggests that her way of dealing with loss is through physical change and new beginnings.

Another major moment of loss in the play is when Christopher finds out two difficult truths: first, that his mother is alive, and second, that Ed killed Wellington. This causes a deep loss of trust. Christopher says, “Father killed Wellington who is a dog and so that meant that he could kill me”. These words are heartbreaking. They show how betrayal can make someone feel unsafe, even around people they love. As a result, Christopher makes a huge decision: he leaves home and travels alone to London. This journey is full of danger and fear, but he handles it using careful planning and logic. Even when his pet rat, Toby, escapes on the train tracks, Christopher shows bravery and determination. This moment shows how far he is willing to go for those he loves, even in the middle of grief and confusion.

The play’s form and structure also help show the effects of loss. Stephens uses Siobhan as a narrator and guide, helping the audience understand Christopher’s thoughts. Because Christopher finds it hard to express emotions, Siobhan’s voice gives us extra insight into how he feels. The play’s non-linear structure (with flashbacks and quick scene changes) also reflects how grief can feel confusing and overwhelming.

In conclusion, Stephens presents loss as something that affects everyone in different ways. Whether it is the death of a pet, the collapse of a marriage, or the breakdown of trust between father and son, each character must find their own way to cope. Christopher uses logic and routines. Ed struggles with guilt and tries to make up for it. Judy acts quickly to protect what matters to her. The play does not offer simple answers but instead shows that grief is complex and deeply human. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This essay is a confident and perceptive exploration of the various forms of loss depicted in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time. It shows a critical style and personal engagement, covering multiple characters and types of loss in detail. Each paragraph offers a clear, thoughtful response, supported with well-chosen and accurate textual references. The student shows assured understanding of how Stephens uses dramatic form (especially narration and structure) to convey emotion. > > The essay is well structured, fluent and sustains a focused argument throughout. parts.problem_md:
How is Christopher presented in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Stephens presents Christopher as an unusual and deeply honest narrator-hero whose literal, logical way of seeing the world both isolates him and allows him to achieve extraordinary things.

Stephens establishes Christopher’s character through his precise, factual way of speaking. He introduces himself by stating that he knows “all the countries of the world and the capital cities” and “every prime number up to 7507”. The exactness of “7507” rather than a round number captures how Christopher’s mind works in precise facts. He also insists “I do not tell lies”, simply because he “can’t tell lies”, which makes him a completely reliable narrator and invites the audience to trust and sympathise with him from the start.

Stephens also presents Christopher as someone who struggles to understand other people. Christopher admits “I find people confusing”, explaining that “people do a lot of talking without using any words”. By having Christopher describe ordinary social signals, such as a raised eyebrow, as if they were a foreign code, Stephens lets the audience see the world from his point of view and understand why everyday interactions overwhelm him. This honesty about his difficulties makes him sympathetic rather than strange.

The play’s most striking feature is its form: Christopher’s teacher Siobhan reads aloud from the book he has written, and the cast act it out around him. Stephens uses this play-within-a-play structure to put Christopher’s mind directly on stage. The set, often a grid of squares and numbers, reflects the way Christopher organises the world, and his habit of numbering the chapters with prime numbers becomes the structure of the story itself. This form lets the audience experience Christopher’s logical, mathematical way of thinking rather than just hearing about it.

Stephens uses stagecraft to dramatise how Christopher experiences the world. When he is touched or overwhelmed, the stage erupts with noise, flashing lights and overlapping voices, especially during the terrifying journey through the London Underground. These moments use sound and lighting to put the audience inside Christopher’s panic, making them feel his distress rather than simply watch it. Stephens turns Christopher’s heightened senses into powerful theatre.

Despite his difficulties, Christopher is presented as quietly heroic. His investigation into the killing of Wellington the dog, and his solo journey to London to find his mother, show enormous courage for someone who finds the world so frightening. Stephens makes the audience admire him precisely because each small action — asking neighbours questions, getting on a train alone — costs him so much. By staging these ordinary tasks as huge obstacles, Stephens reframes courage as something measured not by how easy an act is, but by how much fear a character overcomes to do it. His refusal to lie also drives the plot: because Christopher cannot accept comforting untruths, he keeps digging until he uncovers his father’s lie that his mother had died, so the very honesty that sets him apart becomes the force that exposes the adults’ deceptions and pushes the story towards its crisis.

Structurally, the play builds towards Christopher’s triumph, and Stephens uses his success in maths to show his growing self-belief. When he learns he has passed his A level he announces simply, “I got an A”, and the plain statement carries enormous pride because the audience knows how much he has had to overcome. His repeated, hopeful question, “Does that mean I can do anything?”, ends the play on a note of fragile confidence. Stephens leaves this question hanging rather than answering it, so the audience is encouraged to believe in Christopher even as it sees how much the world still frightens him.

Through Christopher’s honest narration, the inventive play-within-a-play form and its bold stagecraft, Stephens presents a hero unlike any other. He encourages the audience not to pity Christopher but to admire him, showing that a mind which works differently can be a source of remarkable courage, logic and truth.

> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The answer keeps a clear focus on how Christopher is presented rather than retelling the plot, moving from his voice to his difficulties, the play’s form, its stagecraft and his courage. References are short and embedded (“every prime number up to 7507”, “I find people confusing”, “I do not tell lies”), and form and structure are genuinely analysed: the play-within-a-play device, the prime-number chapters, and the use of sound and light to dramatise Christopher’s senses.
>

>

> - A response could focus on Christopher’s relationships with Ed and Siobhan, exploring how Stephens uses them to show Christopher’s need for honesty and trust.

parts.problem_md:
How are Mr and Mrs Shears important in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Although Mr and Mrs Shears appear only briefly, Stephens makes them hugely important, because between them they trigger the play's central mystery and reveal the truth about Christopher's broken family.

Mrs Shears matters first because her dog's death sets the whole play in motion. The opening stage direction — "A dead dog lies in the middle of the stage. A large garden fork is sticking out of its side" — gives the audience a shocking visual image before anyone speaks, and that dog belongs to Mrs Shears, described by Christopher as "our friend". Stephens uses this killing as the inciting incident: Christopher decides "I am going to find out who killed Wellington", and his investigation becomes the spine of the play. Without Mrs Shears and her dog, there is no detective story and no "book" for Christopher to write.

Mr Shears is important in a different way — he is the absent man behind the family's collapse. Christopher's detective logic names him early as his "Prime Suspect", because he "divorced Mrs Shears and left her". Dramatically, Stephens keeps Mr Shears mostly off-stage and talked about rather than seen, which makes him feel like a threatening, mysterious figure. The strength of feeling around him appears through Ed, who refuses to have "that man's name mentioned in my house" and snaps that "that man is evil". This intense reaction signals to the audience that Mr Shears is tied to something painful long before the truth comes out.

Together, the Shears expose the secret at the heart of the play. Through Mrs Alexander, Christopher learns that his mother was "very good friends with Mr Shears", and Siobhan's careful question about whether "your mother and Mr Shears had an affair" confirms it. Stephens uses dramatic irony here: the audience pieces the affair together alongside Christopher, sharing his slow, painful realisation. So the two Shears are structurally vital — Mrs Shears' dog begins the search for one truth, the killer, while Mr Shears turns out to be linked to a far bigger truth: why Christopher's mother really left.

The Shears also matter because they represent the messy adult relationships Christopher struggles to understand. Ed's confession reveals that Mrs Shears "helped me through a very difficult time" after Judy left, and that their friendship broke down because, as Ed bitterly puts it, she "cared more for that bloody dog than for us". This tangle of need, jealousy and resentment is exactly the kind of emotional world Christopher finds confusing. Stephens uses the Shears as a contrast to Christopher's literal, logical mind, highlighting the gap between his clear way of seeing and the complicated feelings of the adults around him.

The way Stephens presents the Shears adds to their importance. Because the whole play is staged as Christopher's "book" being read aloud by his teacher Siobhan, the Shears reach the audience filtered through Christopher's eyes and the words of other characters. We rarely hear directly from them; instead they are described, quoted and judged by others. This method makes them feel less like rounded people and more like pieces in Christopher's puzzle, which suits the detective structure and keeps the focus on how their actions affect Christopher rather than on their own feelings.

So although neither character is on stage for long, Stephens makes Mr and Mrs Shears essential. Mrs Shears' dog launches the plot, Mr Shears unlocks the family secret, and between them they reveal the adult world of love and betrayal that Christopher must slowly learn to navigate.

> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The response stays focused on why the Shears are important and ranges across the whole play — from the opening image of Wellington to Ed's confession — rather than retelling the plot. References are short and embedded ("our friend", "Prime Suspect", "that man is evil"), and dramatic methods are analysed rather than just mentioned: the opening stage image, the choice to keep Mr Shears off-stage, dramatic irony, and the framing of the story as Christopher's narrated "book".
> 
> The answer keeps a clear personal line of argument — that the Shears matter structurally and thematically despite little stage time — and supports it with discriminating detail. This sustained focus on form and structure, expressed in a confident student voice, is what secures Level 5.
> 
> **Other arguments you could consider**
> 
> - A response could focus more on Mrs Shears alone, exploring how her grief and anger after Wellington's death drive the early scenes and Christopher's sense of injustice.
> - A response could argue that the Shears are important mainly as a contrast, using them to show how differently Christopher and the adults handle relationships and truth.

parts.problem_md:
Ed (talking to Christopher): “You have to know that I am going to tell you the truth from now on.”

Explore the significance of truth and lies in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Stephens makes truth and lies the moral centre of the play, contrasting Christopher's complete honesty with the damaging lies of the adults around him, and showing that trust can only be rebuilt through the truth.

From the start, Stephens presents Christopher as someone for whom lying is impossible. Through Siobhan reading his words, he explains "I do not tell lies", adding that "It is because I can't tell lies" rather than because he is good. This honesty is part of how his mind works: he needs the world to be factual and ordered. The form of the play reinforces this, since the whole story is staged as Christopher's truthful "book", read aloud by Siobhan, so the audience is constantly reminded that what we watch is his honest account. Stephens uses Christopher's literal truthfulness as a measuring stick against which every other character's dishonesty is judged.

The biggest lie in the play is Ed's. To protect Christopher, he claims "your mother's died", when in fact she has left for London with Mr Shears. Stephens builds this lie in stages — first that she has "had to go into hospital", then that she has died — so the audience watches a loving father bury the truth deeper and deeper. The lie is well-meant but devastating, and it shapes Christopher's whole understanding of his family until he discovers his mother's hidden letters.

The turning point comes when Christopher finds the letters and realises the truth. He states plainly, "Father lied to me. And also he killed Wellington and so that means that he could kill me." Stephens uses Christopher's flat, logical voice to make the moment more powerful: he reasons his way coldly from one lie to a terrifying conclusion. The detective structure of the play means the search for who killed Wellington leads directly to this bigger truth about the family, so the two mysteries are tied together and the audience uncovers both alongside Christopher.

The play's most important scene about truth is Ed's confession. He admits "I killed Wellington, Christopher" and tries to explain himself, but first he makes a promise: "You have to know that I am going to tell you the truth from now on." Stephens gives Ed a long, broken monologue full of pauses, which makes his honesty feel painful and genuine. Ed even admits "It's bloody hard telling the truth all the time", showing that truth-telling is an effort rather than something easy. Crucially, Christopher does not forgive him at once — he screams and pushes Ed away — because trust, once broken by lies, cannot be repaired instantly.

Stephens shows that lies, even kind ones, do real damage, while truth is the only path back to trust. Ed warns that "if you don't tell the truth now, then later on it hurts even more", a line that sums up the play's message. By the end, Ed slowly earns back Christopher's trust through small, honest actions, and the play closes on cautious hope rather than punishment. The structure moves from a web of lies towards gradual honesty, suggesting that relationships survive not by hiding the truth but by facing it.

Through Christopher's inability to lie, Ed's damaging deception and the slow rebuilding that follows, Stephens makes truth and lies the heart of the play. He shows that lies told out of love still wound, and that trust can only grow again on honest ground.

References are short and embedded ("I do not tell lies", "your mother's died", "I killed Wellington, Christopher"), and dramatic methods are analysed: Christopher's flat narrative voice, dramatic irony as the audience uncovers the lie, and Ed's long, broken confession monologue.
>

parts.problem_md:
Discuss the presentation of Christopher's relationship with animals in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Stephens presents Christopher as someone who trusts and understands animals far more easily than people, using his bond with animals to reveal both his loneliness and his need for a simple, honest world.

From early on, Christopher states simply "I like dogs" and insists "I think dogs are important too". Stephens shows that animals make sense to Christopher in a way people do not: they are predictable and do not lie or hide their feelings. This links to his wider character, since he finds human emotions and social rules confusing and frightening. His preference for animals is part of how Stephens presents Christopher's unusual, logical way of seeing the world.

Stephens opens the play with a powerful stage image built around an animal. Before anyone speaks, the audience sees "a dead dog" with "a large garden fork" sticking out of it, and Christopher standing silently beside it. Stephens uses this shocking opening tableau, and the long silence that follows, to make the dead animal the emotional centre of the play from its first moment. By placing Christopher next to the body rather than having him explain it, Stephens shows how much the animal matters to him before we even understand his character, so the audience’s sympathy is tied to Christopher’s care for the dog from the very start.

Christopher's clearest relationship is with his pet rat, Toby. He lists "looking after Toby" among the things he loves most, and even imagines taking the rat into space, saying he "would like it if I could take Toby with me". Stephens uses Toby to show Christopher's caring, responsible side: he looks after the animal faithfully, and the rat becomes a source of comfort and companionship. When Christopher later makes the terrifying journey to London alone, taking Toby with him shows how the animal is a steady, trusted presence in a confusing human world.

Christopher's bond with animals also drives the plot. The play opens with the disturbing image of Wellington, "a dead dog" with "a large garden fork ... sticking out of its side", and it is Christopher's care for the animal that makes him determined: "I am going to find out who killed Wellington." Stephens makes this animal death the inciting incident, and Christopher's sense that the dog deserves justice launches his detective "book". His reaction shows that he feels a strong moral duty towards animals, arguably stronger than the duty the adults around him feel.

Animals matter to Christopher because they never betray him, unlike the people who do. The deepest wound in the play is that his father "killed Wellington", and Christopher's cold logic — that someone who could kill a dog "could kill me" — shows how closely he links cruelty to animals with danger and broken trust. Stephens uses this to make the killing of a dog feel as serious as a crime against a person, because for Christopher animals are honest creatures who deserve protection. The fact that the lie about his mother and the killing of the dog come from the same person makes his sense of betrayal complete.

Christopher's love of animals connects to his love of being alone. He explains that he "really like[s] little spaces so long as there is no one else in them with me", and his dream of being an astronaut is partly a dream of a calm world without confusing people. Stephens stages the play as Christopher's "book", with Siobhan reading his words aloud, so the audience hears his fondness for animals directly in his own honest voice. This form keeps us close to Christopher's feelings and helps us understand why simple, loyal animals matter so much to him.

Through Toby, Wellington and his clear preference for animals over people, Stephens presents Christopher's relationship with animals as a window into his character. Animals give him the honesty, loyalty and calm that he cannot always find in the human world.

Ed (talking about Christopher): “I cooked his meals. I cleaned his clothes. I looked after him every weekend.”

Explore the idea of looking after others in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Stephens presents looking after others as one of the play's central concerns, showing through Ed, Siobhan and Christopher himself that real care is difficult, practical and often unappreciated, but deeply important.

Ed is the clearest example of looking after others. As a single father, his love for Christopher shows in everyday actions rather than words. In his angry, hurt speech he lists everything he has done: "I cooked his meals. I cleaned his clothes. I looked after him every weekend." Stephens uses this pile-up of short, plain sentences to show how much practical care Ed has given, and how exhausted and unappreciated he feels. The repeated "I" hammers home that, for Ed, love means daily, unglamorous effort that nobody notices.

Stephens shows that looking after Christopher is genuinely hard, which makes Ed's care more real. Judy's letters admit that she "couldn't take it any more" and left, while Ed stayed. Even Ed reaches breaking point: his lie about Christopher's mother and his killing of Wellington come partly from the strain of coping alone for years. Stephens does not present Ed as a perfect carer but as a flawed, struggling one, and this makes his devotion more believable and moving than an easy, idealised love would be.

Christopher's teacher Siobhan looks after him in a gentler, different way. Throughout the play she helps him understand his own feelings and the confusing behaviour of others. Stephens gives her a special role in the play's form: she reads Christopher's "book" aloud and often speaks directly to the audience, guiding both Christopher and us through the story. Her calm, patient support shows a kind of care based on understanding rather than just practical tasks, and she becomes a steady, trusted figure when the adults in his family let him down.

Looking after others is not only something done to Christopher; he does it too. He cares devotedly for his pet rat, listing "looking after Toby" as one of the things he loves most, and refuses to leave the animal behind when he travels. His determination to win justice for the murdered Wellington is also a kind of care. Stephens uses these moments to show that Christopher, so often seen as someone who only needs looking after, is himself loyal and protective towards the creatures he loves. His care is fierce and uncomplicated, a quiet contrast to the messy, strained care the adults around him struggle to give.

Stephens uses the play's structure to show that the role of carer has to be earned back once it is broken. After Christopher learns the truth, he no longer trusts his father, and Ed can only begin to repair their relationship through a promise and a small, careful action. Ed swears, "I promise I will never do anything like that again", and later gives Christopher a puppy he names Sandy. Stephens makes the gift of an animal Ed's way of proving he can be trusted to look after something again, so that the play ends with care being slowly rebuilt rather than simply restored. This quiet, hopeful resolution shows that looking after others depends on patience as much as effort.

Stephens links looking after others to honesty and trust. Ed's care is almost destroyed by his lies, and he can only begin to put things right by promising the truth and slowly proving, through small actions, that Christopher can rely on him again. The play's structure moves from this broken trust towards a fragile, hopeful repair. By staging the story as Christopher's own account, read by Siobhan, Stephens keeps the audience close to Christopher's experience of being looked after — and of learning to look after others in return.

Through Ed's practical devotion, Siobhan's patient guidance and Christopher's love for Toby, Stephens presents looking after others as demanding and imperfect but essential. The play suggests that real care is shown not in words but in steady, everyday actions — and that it depends on trust.
